mappings.note: Is nutrition a necessity for an organism? Argues why food is required at all -- the nutrition strand of C 3.2-LO-1, not respiration or transport.

What happens if green plants disappear. The answer runs through food chains and the collapse of consumers, which is organisms-to-ecosystems reasoning (C 4.3), not a question about how one organism nourishes itself (C 3.2-LO-1).
Leaves coated with vaseline: stomata are blocked so gas exchange and transpiration both stop. Two processes at once, so the competency C 3.2; C 4.3-LO-1 would cover only the transpiration half.
How aerobic respiration differs from anaerobic -- C 3.2-LO-3 verbatim.

Matching item: phloem with translocation is plant transport (C 4.3-LO-1); nephron with excretion, veins with deoxygenated blood and platelets with clotting are the human transport and excretion pathway (C 3.2-LO-2). Both cited because the four pairs split across the two.
Differentiate artery from vein -- vessels of the human transport system, C 3.2-LO-2.
Adaptations of the leaf for photosynthesis. Structure-to-function, but C 4.2-LO-1 names only the alveolus, nephron and villus, so the correct home is the autotrophic-nutrition outcome C 3.2-LO-1.
Why a herbivore's small intestine is longer -- cellulose takes longer to digest. A nutrition-strategy comparison, C 3.2-LO-1, not C 4.2-LO-1, which is about the villus rather than gut length.
What happens without gastric mucus -- the stomach wall is digested by its own acid and pepsin. A step of human digestion, C 3.2-LO-1.
Significance of emulsification -- bile breaks fat into droplets so lipase can act. Human digestion, C 3.2-LO-1.
What moves food along the alimentary canal -- peristalsis. Part of the human nutrition sequence, C 3.2-LO-1.

Why absorption happens mainly in the small intestine -- villi give it the surface area. C 4.2-LO-1 names the villus and is the structure-to-function outcome; qid:85602 is the same idea and is mapped the same way.
Matching autotrophic/heterotrophic/parasitic/food-vacuole nutrition to green plant, deer, leech and Paramoecium. Entirely the nutrition-mode outcome C 3.2-LO-1.
Why aquatic organisms breathe faster -- dissolved oxygen is scarcer than atmospheric. A cross-organism respiration comparison, so the competency rather than the human-only LO-2.
Why human circulation is called double -- blood passes through the heart twice per cycle. C 3.2-LO-2.
Major events during photosynthesis -- light absorption, water splitting, CO2 reduction. Autotrophic nutrition, C 3.2-LO-1.

Predict the rate of photosynthesis on cloudy days, without rainfall, after manuring and with dirt-blocked stomata. The content is autotrophic nutrition (C 3.2-LO-1); changing one factor at a time and predicting the outcome is C 8.1.
What Cuscuta, ticks and leeches share -- all are parasites. A nutrition-mode classification, C 3.2-LO-1; C 4.1 is not cited because the question groups them by feeding, not into kingdoms.
Role of the mouth cavity in digestion -- chewing and salivary amylase. First step of human nutrition, C 3.2-LO-1.
Functions of the gastric glands -- HCl, pepsin and mucus. Human digestion, C 3.2-LO-1.
Matching trypsin, amylase, bile and pepsin to pancreas, saliva, liver and gastric glands -- enzymes to the glands that secrete them, a step of human nutrition, C 3.2-LO-1.
Correct substrates for trypsin, amylase, pepsin and lipase. Enzyme-to-food-class matching within human digestion, C 3.2-LO-1.
Why veins have thinner walls than arteries -- blood pressure in the two vessel types, C 3.2-LO-2.
What happens without platelets -- no clotting, continued blood loss. Blood is the transport medium named in C 3.2-LO-2.

Why plants need less energy than animals -- they do not move, and have dead supporting tissue. A comparison of life processes between plants and animals, so the competency C 3.2 rather than the respiration LO-3, which is about products and energy yield of one pathway.
Why and how water enters root xylem continuously -- root pressure from ion accumulation and osmosis. Plant transport, C 4.3-LO-1.
Why transpiration matters -- it pulls water up the xylem and cools the plant. C 4.3-LO-1.
How leaves help in excretion -- waste stored in leaves is shed. Plant excretion, which C 3.2 covers; LO-2 is limited to excretion in human beings.
Nutrition in Amoeba -- pseudopodia, food vacuole, intracellular digestion. Heterotrophic nutrition, C 3.2-LO-1.
Describe the human alimentary canal -- the organs of the digestive tract in order, C 3.2-LO-1.
Process of breathing in man -- diaphragm, ribs, pressure changes and the air pathway. C 3.2-LO-2, which names the respiratory pathway and its organs.
How carbohydrates, proteins and fats are digested in humans -- the full digestive sequence, C 3.2-LO-1.
Mechanism of photosynthesis -- autotrophic nutrition, C 3.2-LO-1. C 3.1 is not cited: the question is about the process, not about the chloroplast as an organelle.
The three breakdown pathways of glucose -- aerobic, and the two anaerobic routes to lactic acid and to ethanol. Products and energy released, C 3.2-LO-3.
Flow of blood through the human heart -- chambers and vessels in order, C 3.2-LO-2.

Urine formation in the kidneys -- filtration, reabsorption, secretion. The human excretory pathway, C 3.2-LO-2; C 4.2-LO-1 would be right only if the question were about nephron structure serving its function.

What we take from and give back to the environment, and whether we should degrade it. This is organism-to-environment exchange at the ecosystem level, C 4.3. C 5.2 was considered for the value clause but is reserved here for named case studies of Science in human life.
The two processes basic to life on earth (photosynthesis and respiration) and how they sustain life. Holds both processes together, so the competency C 3.2, not a single-process LO.
Roots need soil air but have no pores -- gas exchange by diffusion through root hairs. Exchange of materials in a plant, C 3.2, since LO-2 is the human respiratory pathway.
Which parts of breathing are active and which passive -- the mechanics of the human breathing cycle, C 3.2-LO-2.
The term for moving food from leaves to the rest of the plant (translocation) -- phloem transport, C 4.3-LO-1.
What transpiration is -- water loss as vapour, the force behind xylem transport, C 4.3-LO-1.
The tissue carrying soluble products of photosynthesis is phloem -- C 4.3-LO-1.
The tissue carrying water and minerals is xylem -- the other half of C 4.3-LO-1, and deliberately the same code as its phloem twin above.
How autotrophs obtain carbon dioxide and nitrogen -- raw-material sourcing for autotrophic nutrition, C 3.2-LO-1.
The pancreatic enzyme that digests protein is trypsin -- human digestion, C 3.2-LO-1.
The salivary enzyme that breaks starch is amylase -- C 3.2-LO-1.
Role of stomach acid. Duplicate of qid:85600 under a different source tag; mapped identically to C 3.2-LO-1 so the pair stays consistent.
Role of saliva in digestion. Duplicate of qid:85618; same code C 3.2-LO-1.
Function of digestive enzymes -- breaking large molecules into absorbable ones, C 3.2-LO-1.
The two ways glucose is oxidised to release energy -- with and without oxygen, C 3.2-LO-3.
Sources of the raw materials for photosynthesis. Duplicate of qid:85599; same code C 3.2-LO-1.
Where fat is digested -- the small intestine, after bile emulsifies it. Human digestion, C 3.2-LO-1.
How bread mould and mushroom feed -- saprophytic nutrition by external digestion. A heterotrophic mode, C 3.2-LO-1.
The blood component that forms a clot is the platelet -- blood as the transport medium, C 3.2-LO-2.
One difference between autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition -- C 3.2-LO-1, the same outcome as qid:85598 and qid:85646.
The process by which plants lose water as vapour is transpiration -- C 4.3-LO-1.
What translocation is in plants -- phloem transport of soluble food, C 4.3-LO-1.

The basic difference between respiration and photosynthesis. Sets two life processes against each other, so the competency C 3.2 rather than LO-1 (nutrition alone) or LO-3 (aerobic vs anaerobic alone).
Intermediate and end products of aerobic glucose breakdown -- pyruvate, then CO2 and water. Products and energy, C 3.2-LO-3.
